nameStory: The 'striped' in this woodlouse's name comes from the distinctive light and dark bands that run across its back, making it look like it's wearing a tiny striped sweater. It's also called the 'fast woodlouse' because unlike its slow-moving cousins, this little crustacean can actually scurry quite quickly when disturbed!
description: The Common Striped Woodlouse is a small, oval-shaped land crustacean that looks like a tiny armored pill bug. Despite its name, it can't actually roll into a complete ball like some of its relatives. These little creatures are typically gray to brown in color with noticeable lighter stripes running across their segmented backs, and they grow to about half an inch long.

idTips.label: Striped pattern
idTips.description: Look for distinct light-colored stripes running crosswise across the dark gray or brown back segments - these bands are quite visible and feel smooth to the touch

idTips.label: Speed and movement
idTips.description: When disturbed, it scurries away much faster than other woodlice - you'll notice it's surprisingly quick and agile for such a small creature

idTips.label: Body shape
idTips.description: Oval and flattened with a smooth, hard shell that feels like touching a small plastic bead - cannot roll into a tight ball when threatened

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: About the size of your pinky nail, typically around half an inch long, with a firm texture when gently handled

idTips.label: Antennae
idTips.description: Two pairs of antennae with the outer pair being noticeably longer and more prominent, constantly moving as it explores

habitat: You'll find Common Striped Woodlice in moist environments throughout New England, particularly under logs, stones, leaf litter, and in garden mulch. They thrive in deciduous and mixed forests where they can hide under decomposing bark and fallen branches. Look for them in your backyard compost pile, under flower pots, or anywhere the soil stays consistently damp.

seasonality.spring: Active and easiest to spot as they emerge from winter hiding spots under logs and stones. This is when you're most likely to see them scurrying around during the day.
seasonality.summer: Most active during humid evenings and after rain showers. During hot, dry days they retreat deep under cover, so check under mulch and stones in the morning.
seasonality.fall: Still quite active as they prepare for winter, often found gathering under thick leaf litter. Great time to observe them as they're busy feeding on decomposing plant material.
seasonality.winter: Hidden deep under logs, stones, and thick organic matter where they remain sluggish but alive. Only visible during mild winter days when temperatures rise above freezing.

funFact: These 'bugs' are actually more closely related to lobsters and crabs than to insects - they're land-dwelling crustaceans that still breathe through gill-like structures and need moisture to survive, making them some of the few crustaceans that have successfully made the transition from sea to land!
confusionNotes: Often confused with pill bugs (roly-polies), but striped woodlice can't roll into a complete ball and have those distinctive stripes. Remember: 'Stripes that can't make spheres' - if it has stripes and can't roll up tight, it's likely your striped woodlouse!
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'woodlice,' these creatures aren't actually lice at all - the name is a holdover from when people thought any small crawling creature was some type of louse. They're beneficial decomposers that help break down organic matter in your garden, so they're actually helpful to have around!
compareHints: Since this is the only Philoscia species commonly found in New England, compare it to other woodlice families in the region. Unlike pill bugs (Armadillidiidae), striped woodlice cannot roll into a complete ball and have more obvious striping. Unlike common rough woodlice, they're much faster moving and have smoother, more distinct striped patterns rather than mottled coloring.
